subject: Request: Dedicated SLA amendment for buffering policy and latency floor
messages:
From: Samantha Lowe <samantha@oraq.com>
To: rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai
Cc: procurement@oraq.com
Date: Sat, 15 May 2027 09:12:00 -0700
Subject: SLA request: buffering policy and latency floor for dedicated pool

Hi Rishi,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We’re close to an approval from engineering, but procurement and SRE need one more piece: written SLA language or an exception that covers how Redwood will handle short, high-intensity inference spikes for our dedicated pool.

Background: our product issues fan-out inference requests during end-of-day indexing windows (roughly 10–30 minutes), where QPS can jump 6–8x. During those windows P95 stays fine but P99/P99.9 tails spike and that materially impacts user-visible latency. We need either:

- a buffering/bursting policy that guarantees a latency floor (e.g., P99.9 < 180ms) for sustained spikes up to X QPS for Y minutes, or
- a standby reservation model (hot standby GPUs) that we can pay for but only consume during bursts.

What procurement needs in the SOW: explicit queueing behavior (how requests are queued and prioritized), what counts as an SLA breach (time windows, measurement method), and remedies (service credits). Also please share the technical doc that explains preemption/eviction behavior for dedicated pools.

I’ve attached a sample SLA matrix the legal team provided as a template. Can you let me know if Redwood can accommodate an amendment or a carve-out and what the cost delta would look like?

Thanks,
Samantha Lowe
Head of Platform Reliability
Oraq Systems

(attachment: oraq_sla_matrix.xlsx)

From: rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai
To: Samantha Lowe <samantha@oraq.com>
Cc: marissa.cole@redwood.ai, procurement@oraq.com
Date: Sat, 15 May 2027 11:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA request: buffering policy and latency floor for dedicated pool

Hi Samantha — thanks for the clear ask and the matrix. I’ll coordinate internally and get you a proposal this week.

Quick answers: we can offer an architecture that combines reserved headroom + a prioritized queue for critical traffic. There are two levers we typically surface:

- Burst reservation (hot standby GPUs) — guaranteed capacity you pay for as a standby; immediate tail improvement during bursts.
- Priority buckets + pre-warming — lower-cost but depends on queueing behavior and can add a small extra delay for low-priority jobs.

I’ve looped in Marissa (solutions) and Diego (runtime PM) to scope the techno-legal language and to ask for an estimate on cost delta. Can you confirm the typical peak QPS and how long the peaks last? The CSV in the attachment (oraq_peak_shapes.csv) would help.

I attached a short template that we can start from and will follow up with a draft amendment.

Best,
Rishi Malhotra
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai

(attachment: oraq_sla_matrix.xlsx)

From: marissa.cole@redwood.ai
To: Samantha Lowe <samantha@oraq.com>, rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai
Date: Sun, 16 May 2027 10:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA request: buffering policy and latency floor for dedicated pool

Hi Samantha — good context, thanks. A few practical notes from the SE side:

- Priority buckets: we can surface an ALPHA feature called priority buckets which assigns a higher dispatch priority to a named traffic class (up to 3 levels). This reduces head-of-line blocking for critical requests but does not eliminate backend saturation if the overall node pool is exhausted.

- Burst reservation model: we usually size the hot standby to cover X% of historical peak delta. For a 6–8x spike, we’d recommend standby ~30–40% of peak rather than full replication, combined with short-term autoscale to absorb the rest.

- Measurement: we compute SLAs on production telemetry aggregated by pod and model variant; P99.9 is computed over 1-minute sliding windows (standard in our reporting). For the amendment language we suggest: measurement windows, required tagging of critical traffic, and an explicit duration cap (e.g., up to 45 minutes per rolling 24h).

I’m attaching a runbook excerpt that explains tail-latency mitigation techniques we’ve run in pilots. We can run a short bench with your traffic traces to recommend exact sizing.

—Marissa
Marissa Cole
Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
(attachment: tail_latency_runbook.pdf)

From: diego.fernandez@redwood.ai
To: rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai, marissa.cole@redwood.ai, Samantha Lowe <samantha@oraq.com>
Date: Sun, 16 May 2027 15:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA request: buffering policy and latency floor for dedicated pool

Thanks for the signal, Samantha. Some engineering constraints to call out so legal has realistic expectations:

- Dedicated reserved GPUs give you predictable throughput at the node level (tokens/sec or inference calls/sec depends on model and batch sizing). However, the runtime still queues requests into per-model dispatchers; when utilization approaches 100% you will see queuing growth. Guarantees for tail latency at very high utilization require either capacity over-provisioning (headroom) or explicit burst capacity that is owned by the tenant.

- Preemption & maintenance: we schedule maintenance windows and notify customers; emergency preemption is extremely rare but possible for hardware failures. We can list scheduled maintenance carve-outs in the amendment but cannot fully guarantee zero interruptions in catastrophic failure scenarios.

- Suggested amendment language (draft summary):
  * Redwood will maintain dedicated capacity equal to the committed units (X GPUs) and an optional burst reservation of Y GPUs for up to Z minutes per event.
  * For traffic tagged as "priority-critical", Redwood will attempt to maintain P99.9 latency < 180ms during burst events when burst reservation is available. Measured over 1-minute sliding windows.
  * Remedies: service credits based on minutes of breach beyond the agreed burst window. Credits capped at N% of monthly fee.

To size the proposal I need:
 1) target P99.9 threshold you want (you suggested 180ms),
 2) expected sustained QPS during a peak, and
 3) the percent of traffic that will be tagged as priority-critical.

If you can paste a short sample of the CSV peaks (time, qps) I’ll run a quick model and share estimates tomorrow.

—Diego Fernandez
Product Manager, Serving Runtime
(attachment: none)

From: Samantha Lowe <samantha@oraq.com>
To: diego.fernandez@redwood.ai, rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai
Cc: Ian Brooks <ian.brooks@oraq.com>, procurement@oraq.com
Date: Mon, 17 May 2027 09:02:00 -0700
Subject: Re: SLA request: buffering policy and latency floor for dedicated pool

Diego/Team — thanks, that all sounds reasonable. Attached a CSV with three representative peak windows; the biggest is ~7x baseline and lasts ~22 minutes. Most of the critical traffic is ~12% of total QPS and will be tagged.

Procurement wants: (1) explicit carveout language for scheduled maintenance windows, (2) definition of a breach and a simple credit formula (e.g., 5 minutes breach = 0.5% monthly credit), and (3) an initial pilot period (30 days) where we can validate the sizing before committing to a long-term reserved standby.

We prefer written amendment language to be worded as a short addendum to the Dedicated SLA rather than a separate contract. Can you put together a short amendment (1–2 pages) outlining: committed units, burst reservation sizing and cost, breach definition, monitoring method, and pilot terms?

Thanks — I’ve attached the peaks file.
Samantha
(attachment: oraq_peak_shapes.csv)

1) Diego and Marissa will size a pilot configuration (recommended: 25% standby GPUs + priority queue) and provide an estimated monthly delta by EOD tomorrow.
2) I’ll draft a 1–2 page amendment for the Dedicated SLA that: commits to X dedicated GPUs, defines burst reservation (Y GPUs, Z minutes per event), sets measurement windows (1-minute sliding, P99.9), includes scheduled maintenance carve-outs, and a simple credit formula tied to minutes of breach.
3) Pilot: 30-day validation window with a one-time pilot fee refundable against the annual commitment if you proceed.

If that sounds good I’ll circulate the amendment for legal review and share a Doc link (internal tracker: https://app.hubspot.com/deal/1293).
